title: John Lennon signs documents to dissolve The Beatles’ partnership | 1974
content:
John Lennon had failed to attend a meeting on 19 December 1974 in New York City with Paul McCartney, and George Harrison, to sign documents that would dissolve The Beatles’ legal partnership and allow the official receiver to divide up and distribute royalties which had been frozen since early 1971.

Ten days later Lennon finally signed the documents. It took place at Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida, where he was holidaying with son Julian and partner May Pang.

They stayed at music executive Morris Levy’s apartment in West Palm Beach, at the Sun and Surf complex on Sunrise Avenue. They first visited Walt Disney World on 27 December, and returned two days later, staying at the Polynesian Village Resort Hotel.

We went to Disneyland [sic] on what must have been the most crowded day of the year. It’s funny. I was sitting on the monorail along with everyone else, not being recognised, and I heard someone with his back to me say that George Harrison was there today. The guy was leaning on me at the time, and he’d heard that a Beatle was there somewhere. He couldn’t see the wood for the trees.
John Lennon
Melody Maker, 8 March 1975

Lennon finally agreed to sign the dissolution documents, which were couriered to their hotel room. Also present was Lennon’s lawyer Harold Seider and a representative for The Beatles.

Lennon asked Pang to document the moment with her camera.

We were on our Christmas holiday with Julian Lennon and also Roulette Records’ Morris Levy and his son Adam. John coaxed me into taking a couple of photographs of him signing the papers. He was the last signature to be inked. We were staying at the Polynesian Hotel. Many have speculated which room… I will tell you, we were not on the main floor and not opposite an exit door and no pool outside our room.
May Pang, 29 December 2014
Facebook

The dissolution meant that some solo recordings and other projects could finally be allocated to the former Beatle who worked on them.

In a nutshell, what was arranged was that everybody gets their own individual monies. Even up till this year, till the settlement was signed, all the monies were going into one pot. All individual records, mine, Ringo’s, Paul’s – all into one big pot. It had to go through this big machinery and then come out to us, eventually. So now, even the old Beatle royalties, everything goes into four separate accounts instead of one big pot all the time. That’s that. The rest of it was ground rules. Everybody said the Beatles’ve signed this paper, that means they’re no longer tied in any way. That’s bullshit. We still own this thing called Apple. Which, you can explain, is a bank. A bank the money goes into. But there’s still the entity itself known as the Beatles. The product, the name, the likeness, the Apple thing itself, which still exists, and we still have to communicate on it and make decisions on it and decide who’s to run Apple and who’s to do what. It’s not as cut and dried as the papers said.
John Lennon
Rolling Stone, 5 June 1975
